column1: Academic and Political Contexts
For over a decade
column2: experts have been warning of the dire state of the humanities in the U.S. academy ;;. An emphasis on STEM fields beginning in the early 2010s led many to question the value of the humanities
column3: an attitude reinforced by political leaders who have openly denounced humanities fields as impractical and politically suspect. The increasing cost of higher education and uncertain economic conditions have led students wary of debt and fearing limited future opportunities to choose majors that lead to specific professional fields. In some states
column4: performance funding metrics encourage institutional policies at public universities that disadvantage humanities fields
column5: and recent attacks on diversity
column6: equity and inclusion in higher education have placed restrictions on humanities curriculum and faculty speech. Declining enrollments in humanities majors provide a justification for defunding and eliminating critical programs in languages
column7: literatures
column8: and the arts
column9: in particular.

column1: The recent decline in the humanities in the U.S. academy is part of a long trend. As Eric Adler notes
column2: the present circumstances reflect the continuation of a pattern of privileging practical education that dates from the late nineteenth century: As proponents of the humanities have noted for over a century
column3: the humanistic disciplines were likely to wither in a system deliberately created to marginalize them . We may have reached a critical point in that process today
column4: however
column5: with some suggesting that the humanities may disappear from higher education altogether. On a recent episode of the New York Times podcast Hard Fork
column6: for instance
column7: historian D. Graham Burnett proposed that such an outcome is possible because the shifting economics of education have led administrators
column8: parents and students to all focus on the return on [...] tuition investment and an increasingly exigent job market. Burnett suggests that the humanities must find other contexts in which to survive: the most important forms of that work are going to need to happen outside of colleges and universities .

column1: As rapid social and technological transformation have created new challenges in recent years
column2: the humanities have often not helped themselves by seeming resistant to change. Many scholars engage with today’s world but often do so using traditional methods and creating familiar types of products
column3: usually books and scholarly articles
column4: often working in isolation. To some extent
column5: this is inevitable
column6: as institutional structures and disciplinary expectations reward the production of traditional scholarly outputs while disincentivizing experimentation. The situation is exacerbated by the scarcity of tenure-track positions and the resulting exclusion of talented young scholars who could provide vision needed to transform our fields.

column2: in particular
column3: can often feel out of step with realities beyond the academy. We frequently adhere to traditional methods that ignore students' concerns over economic insecurity
column4: do not effectively respond to a societal climate of anti-intellectualism
column5: and fail to put pressure on entrenched institutional approaches. Our classrooms remain essential spaces for learning to think critically
column6: communicate effectively

column8: and appreciate differences
column9: but our students often lack access to the applied learning that might help them connect with communities
column10: imagine their future professional selves and prepare for their lives after graduation.

column2: the advent of widely available artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT have added another layer of complexity to what already feels like a grim situation. Big Tech's pursuit of developing human-like intelligence feels dystopian and is
column3: as authors  signal

column5: some researchers assert that the humanities
column6: as fields that deal with the complexities of being human

column4: observing that research related to AI has opened up new possibilities for conversation and collaboration between computing
column5: engineering
column6: and the humanities . Dubreuil and Klein et. al. advocate not only for more equitable interdisciplinary partnerships in our research and teaching
column7: but for academic spaces in which humanities scholarship is viewed as central to addressing the many challenges facing human societies today.

column1: Those whose professional activity revolves around the teaching of language and cultures
column2: in particular
column3: may reasonably question such optimism
column4: however. The Modern Language Association reported a 29.3% drop in language enrollments between 2009 and 2021 ()

column6: journalist Louise Matsakis reflected on watching a video of herself talking in perfect Chinese that she had generated using AI . Apple instructs users to [b]ridge language barriers in person — while traveling or navigating in a foreign country — with AirPods . A growing perception that language study is increasingly unnecessary in this context
column7: combined with the emphasis on cost cutting and efficiency that is driving decisions at institutions
column8: offers a grim outlook for language programs across the U.S. . Following the cancellation of all language programs at West Virginia University in 2023

column1: We also find ourselves in a time when the embrace of other cultures at the heart of much humanities scholarship is under attack. In recent years
column2: resentments and fears that were once latent have transformed into unabashed and often violent vilification and dehumanization of those who are different and often the most vulnerable among us. Anti-immigrant sentiment and overt racism in the US have surged to levels not seen in decades
column3: a reality that has grown more intense since January of 2025
column4: as the second Trump administration has made anti-immigration action and legislation top priorities.

column2: such as Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz
column3: ” and in facilities abroad
column4: including CECOT (Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo/Terrorism Confinement Center)
column5: a mega-prison in El Salvador ;;.

column2: . Many immigrants have expressed reluctance to leave their homes out of fear of detention
column3: concerns validated by the Supreme Court’s recent approval of enforcement measures that rely on racial profiling ;;.

column1: Students of Latin American origin face challenges not only in broader society but also in the particular context of higher education. They belong to communities that have historically encountered  barriers to entering the system and have struggled to complete degrees
column2: given the financial burdens and family responsibilities that they often must balance with their schoolwork ;;. The dismantling of affirmative action
column3: the defunding of campus initiatives and programs aimed at promoting diversity and inclusion
column4: and the federal government’s recent discontinuation of grants to Hispanic-Serving Institutions () make matters worse for these students
column5: who often cannot see themselves reflected among faculty and their fellow students and fail to find a sense of belonging.

column1: At the same time
column2: the struggles of marginalized groups in Latin America itself continue unabated. In many places
column3: violence against women and LGBTQIA+ individuals has become a normalized backdrop to everyday life. Indigenous communities face discrimination
column4: the destruction of their lands
column5: and sustained efforts to erase them from society. Those of African descent throughout the region must still fight for visibility
column6: justice
column7: and equal participation in societies that have long minimized their contributions or denied their existence. Community leaders and activists who resist injustice are routinely punished and assassinated ;.

column1: In the face of all these realities
column2: the need for new approaches to scholarship in the humanities is more urgent than ever. Scholars must project their activity into public spaces and engage with those outside the academy. They must demonstrate the value of their work. They likewise must provide students with opportunities to gain formative experiences beyond the classroom and help students of Latin American backgrounds find ways to create spaces of their own within higher education and beyond. Those whose work deals with marginalized peoples must build solidarity with those communities and co-create best practices for working together.

column1: This special issue features articles about a collection of digital projects focused on Latin America and Latinx populations that speak to the notion of a more engaged
column2: socially committed humanities. All are dedicated to connecting with communities

column4: and exploring collaborative modes of knowledge creation. They are all built on sophisticated theoretical foundations but carry out their work in accessible spaces in which non-academic publics are invested. Focusing on the meaningful human interaction at the center of the humanities
column5: each of the projects suggests ways that our research and teaching can create shared experiences in which real people cannot be supplanted by technology. They demonstrate ways we can learn ways to intervene in society’s use of technology and shape it through humanistic inquiry.

column1: Conclusion
This special issue showcases a collection of efforts
column2: reflected in digital projects (in-process or finalized) in which technology is critical not on its own terms
column3: but rather for the ways it allows scholars to engage in activities that are essentially non-digital in nature. By arguing that the use of technology can be instrumental — but is not the point — we believe the articles gathered here contribute to highlighting a paradox in the way DH has long been perceived by those outside the field. The “STEM for the humanities” paradigm has attracted administrators and provoked the suspicion of traditional humanities scholars
column4: emphasizing the incorporation of digital tools into humanities scholarship as being
column5: in some way
column6: about technology. The articles gathered here demonstrate ways that much work in the digital humanities today is not fundamentally about technology
column7: but rather about topics that
column8: in some political and institutional contexts
column9: may make decision makers uncomfortable and which our colleagues outside of DH might recognize as representing continuity with the work of the traditional humanities.

column1: Much of DH remains highly computational in nature and much work arguably emerges from questions that are informed more by computer science than the traditional humanities.  The expansion of the field in recent years
column2: however
column3: has brought a greater recognition that DH often involves using digital tools to counter injustice and construct communities
column4: effecting work that points to new ways that the humanities can engage with the public and demonstrate their relevance in a world where the human experience is increasingly devalued. Like many of the projects highlighted here
column5: such efforts often involve students and frequently imply a reconsideration of our collaborations as well as a reevaluation of what we teach
column6: how
column7: and why.

column2: innovation

column5: both within the US and throughout Latin America and the Caribbean. Highlighting
column6: in particular
column7: the work of interdisciplinary scholars of color
column8: women scholars
column9: and early-career scholars
column10: this special issue offers models for designing hands-on
column11: engaged humanities praxis that can better connect with and serve multilingual and multicultural students and diverse communities beyond the academy and across geographies.
